Pele Yoetz 238:1: Letter Nun: Nechamah (Comfort) — It is known that included in the commandment of acts of kindness is comforting mourners. And not only mourners, but for every kind of trouble that befalls a person, it is a commandment to console him and comfort him with words that enter the heart appropriate to the trouble, for one form of comfort is that every trouble could have been worse, and he should give thanks to God and ask before Him to save him from something even more grievous. Thus, if an impure mishap befalls his money, let him be comforted and give thanks that no illness or pain befell his body; and if it did befall his body, let him give thanks that at least the bitterness of death has passed; and if, God forbid, someone dear to him died, let him be comforted that the deceased did not convert or go astray, and did not die a bad or double death, Heaven have mercy, and that surviving offspring remain from him. And for every kind of mishap, whether to his body, his money, or the death of someone dear, let him be comforted and give thanks for the remnant that survived, and ask for mercy that it be preserved in his hand. And let him be wary of weeping over the dead excessively, for they said (Mo'ed Katan 27b) that one who weeps too much is truly weeping for another death [that will follow], and it turns out that he is a shedder of blood, Heaven have mercy.
Pele Yoetz 238:2: And according to right reasoning, it would not be fitting to weep over the dead at all, for what does weeping give or add or profit — even if he were to kill himself, could he bring the deceased back? As King David, peace be upon him, said when his son died, as explained (II Samuel 12), and as Rabbi Chanina said to his wife when their daughter died and he was not weeping over her — she said to him, “Have you sent a hen out of your house?” [i.e., lost so little?] and he answered her, “Blindness and darkness” [meaning weeping only harms one's eyes] (Shabbat 151b). It appears that had he wept, it would have greatly harmed his eyes. But we have only to fulfill the words of our sages, of blessed memory, who said (Mo'ed Katan, ibid.) three days for weeping [are allotted, and no more, except] if he is a great man, a sage, a pious man — according to his greatness, it is permitted to weep more over him, for we find (Deuteronomy 34:8) that they wept for Moses for thirty days.
Pele Yoetz 238:3: And when one weeps for the dead, let him not weep over his own separation from him, his own longing, or that he did not live to see his joy and the like, for all this is vanity and vexation of spirit, for this world is utter vanity, a world of falsehood, while the World to Come is the world of truth. Rather, why should a living man complain — let him overcome his own sin (Lamentations 3:39), reflecting on how, through his own transgression, this trouble came upon him, causing anger and pain to the exalted and uplifted King, who abounds in doing good and whose very nature is to do good; and at a time when a person is in pain, the Divine Presence is in pain — what does the tongue say, etc. And let him grieve that because of the evil the righteous one was gathered [taken from this world], causing him not to give delight to his Creator — this is the pain of Heaven. Let him take this and the like to heart, and be embittered in weeping, and set his heart to repentance, for this is the whole fruit — that a living man complain and overcome his sins, as it is written right after (ibid., v. 40), “Let us search and examine our ways,” etc. And let him also take to heart that perhaps the deceased is undergoing distress of soul, and let him grieve over him and be embittered in weeping, imagining as though he sees the deceased amid a burning flame, and weep and supplicate and ask for mercy for his rest.
Pele Yoetz 238:4: And there is yet another kind of comfort, as our sages, of blessed memory, said, "the trouble of the many is half a comfort." And let him take to heart that many have drunk this cup, and the flame has fallen even on cedars, and how many great men of the world
Pele Yoetz 238:5: and mighty men have had the raging waters, many evils and troubles of various kinds, pass over their heads. Examine this and you will find that every kind of suffering in the world began with great men, and it is not good [i.e., such suffering] to arrive quickly [i.e., it is common and takes its natural course].
Pele Yoetz 238:6: And there is yet another kind of comfort: let him believe with complete faith that nothing evil descends from Heaven, but rather whatever the Merciful One does, He does for the good, and even when it strikes lives, He foresees and beholds to the end of all generations, and His dealings are measured with purpose; therefore one must bless over the evil in the same manner as over the good, for certainly and completely God intended it for good, for Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, did not kill the Egyptian until he had looked to the end of all generations (Shemot Rabbah 1:29), and the Holy One, blessed be He, was patient with Ammon and Moab for the sake of two good doves [i.e., their eventual good descendants, Ruth and Naamah]. And just as it is a commandment to comfort, so it is a commandment to be comforted and to accept Heaven's judgment with love, for the trouble comes immediately from Him who is Master of the world, ruling His world to do with it as He wills, while we are His servants and the sheep of His hand, and for everything we are obligated to thank Him and bless Him. And one who accepts comfort from others, and especially from within himself, demonstrates that he has upright understanding, proper knowledge, and complete faith.
Pele Yoetz 239:1: Nedivut (Generosity) — How good is this good trait of a generous spirit! Good for Heaven and good for humanity, good for oneself and good for others, good for this world and good for the World to Come. This is a gift of God and is a natural disposition in a person; there is one whose soul desires it and who becomes a great spender, and there is a chronic evil where a person has no control over his spirit to make expenditures for his own needs and to sustain his own soul. Happy is the man whom the Lord has graced with a good nature; but as for one whose nature is bad, this is not a way to remove him from transgression, and it does not exempt him from the Day of Judgment, for it is within a person's power, through his own intellect, through diligence in studying ethics, and through constant struggle and strategy, to change his nature and exchange evil for good, for the reward is according to the pain; and let him pour out his soul before the Lord that a generous spirit support him.
Pele Yoetz 239:2: But the difficulty is that the way of a man is right in his own eyes, and he thinks his hand suffices him and he has fulfilled his duty. Thus the Torah has already given a measure for what should properly be done — a moderate measure, a tenth of whatever he has in hand, year by year. Therefore the sages of the parable say, “Come, let us reckon: if you do this, you will be built up in this world and established for the World to Come.”
Pele Yoetz 239:3: And the trait of generosity is also greatly needed toward himself and the members of his household, that he sustain them with judgment, according to the blessing the Lord has given him, and in the manner he makes his expenditures, so the Lord will command his blessing to be with him; but if he has no regard for his own life and that of his household, his Maker will not have mercy on him, for whoever is strict with others is dealt with strictly. And it is known from the parable of the funnel: just as one pours from below, so they pour upon him from above, and if he holds back his finger from below, the one pouring from above will also withdraw His hand. However, these are matters without fixed measure — each person should extend his hand according to his measure, and stretch his leg according to his blanket. And where they said to be sparing, he is not permitted to be generous, and where they said to be generous, he is not permitted to be sparing — for if he sees that his sustenance is limited, he should close his hand, for they said (Shabbat 118a), “Make your Shabbat like a weekday rather than become dependent on people,” and even to give charity and increase in commandments he is not so permitted, for his own life and the lives of his household come first, and all the more so if he has debts owed to fellow Israelites, in which case it is incumbent upon him to conduct himself according to the chapter of “the closed handful is greater” [i.e., strict frugality], both regarding himself, his food, and his clothing, and regarding the members of his household, and he shall live a life of hardship until he pays his debts. And needless to say, he should not increase charity-giving, for it would not be counted to him as charity but rather as a transgression on his part. Therefore it is good for a man to manage his affairs with judgment.
Pele Yoetz 239:4: And part of generosity is that one should not be too exacting in his sale of goods to his fellow or purchase from his fellow, but rather sell cheaply, so that room remains for his fellow to profit too, as our sages, of blessed memory, said. And especially if the other party is a poor man, or a Torah scholar, he should not profit from him but give him even less than its value, and should buy from him at a high price as he asks. And if he hires him for his work, he should pay him more, with a generous eye, and it will be counted to him as great charity, since the recipient is not shamed. Not like many wealthy men who, when they come to buy something from a poor man, or hire him, are exacting over trivial matters of poverty, and say, “When we want to give charity, we know how, but in buying and selling we do not wish to be gracious.” Would that they gain wisdom to understand that there is no charity greater than this, where the poor man thinks he is simply taking what is his own, while it is revealed before Heaven [as an act of charity].
Pele Yoetz 239:5: And part of the trait of generosity is that one should lend out his vessels and not worry about minor loss, for it is a great commandment; therefore let him weigh the reward of a commandment against its loss. And now, through our sins, like the Hebrew women in Egypt [a reference to their stinginess, per midrash], a woman's eye is often stingy about lending her vessels, and they increase quarreling over trivial matters, and it is incumbent upon her husband to guide and lead her so that her eyes be generous. It is known the saying of our sages, of blessed memory (Devarim Rabbah 6:8), that plagues used to come upon the stingy who did not wish to lend their vessels, and one who claimed he had none, Heaven would reveal his sin, and the priest would come and command that the house be cleared and his vessels brought outside, and his disgrace would be revealed. And especially regarding holy books, great generosity is needed — not to withhold good from its owner — but to lend one's books to any who ask and not worry about wear on the binding, for see, this is a great matter that is written in the books (Sefer Chasidim, section 869) that there is a tradition among the holy that whoever does not lend books will not have descendants surviving after him, God forbid. Therefore let a man tremble and not refrain from lending his books, so that wealth and riches be in his house and his righteousness stand forever.
Pele Yoetz 239:6: And part of generosity is that one be generous with his own body, wisdom and counsel, helping every seeker of assistance from him, and not withhold any good that is in his power to do — let him surely do it with a generous eye, whether much or little, according to his ability, for in everything he gives delight to his Creator, and He will repay him.
Pele Yoetz 240:1: Nekimah U'Netirah (Revenge and Grudge-Bearing) — Revenge and grudge-bearing are two commandments about which our Maker warned and commanded us (Leviticus 19:18), “You shall not take vengeance nor bear a grudge against the children of your people.” Our sages, of blessed memory, explained (Yoma 23a) that revenge is one who says, “As he did to me, so shall I do to him — just as he withheld good from me, so I shall withhold it from him.” And grudge-bearing is one who is asked [for a favor] and grants his fellow's request, repaying good instead of evil, but says to him, “See that I am not like you,” in a manner that shows he has not removed it from his heart. And one is obligated not to hold any grudge at all, and all the more so not to rejoice at the fall of an enemy who has done him evil, as ignorant people are accustomed to do — that when some pain or damage befalls one who has done him evil, he immediately says, “This pain is mine to inflict; I punish him,” as though the Holy One, blessed be He, had demanded satisfaction for his honor. Would that they gain wisdom to understand that this is bad for him, for whoever causes his fellow to be punished is not brought into the divisions of the Holy One, blessed be He (Shabbat 149a), and as the Tosafot there explain (22a, s.v. “Ana”), that the great men of the world used to grieve when they said, “I am the cause of his punishment,” fearing that it was because of them that he was punished. Moreover, it is written (Proverbs 17:5), “He who rejoices at calamity will not go unpunished.”
Pele Yoetz 240:2: Now, at first glance, a person might judge by appearance that while the commandment not to take revenge can be fulfilled, not to bear a grudge in the heart and not to rejoice in the heart at the misfortune of an enemy who seeks his harm is impossible, and he might say that this commandment is fitting only for the ministering angels, among whom there is no envy, hatred, or rivalry. But since our Maker commanded us regarding it, we certainly can fulfill it, for the Holy One, blessed be He, does not deal tyrannically with His creatures, and the Torah was not given to the ministering angels, and understanding is easy for one who has sense, and one who reflects on the matter will find a good reason for this commandment, as a living person takes it to heart and believes with complete faith that from the mouth of the Most High come the evils and the good things that befall a person, whether by the hand of Heaven or by human hand, even for the value of a mere perutah, and no person can do harm or good, even for the value of a mere perutah, or honor him or disparage his honor and the like, without a decree of the Almighty; and a person does not so much as bruise his finger below unless it is decreed from above, and the Omnipresent has many agents, and merit comes about through one deserving and guilt through one liable. It follows that whoever does him good or evil, whether to his body, his money, or his honor, is performing an errand of the Merciful One. And when this is firmly fixed in his heart with complete faith, like nails that will not be moved, his heart will understand that he should not blame his fellow, as David, king of Israel, said, “The Lord told him to curse” (II Samuel 16:10), and he [the human agent] is like an axe in the hand of the one who wields it (Isaiah 10:15), and in the end that agent will receive his own due from the One who sent him, in the manner of what is written (ibid., v. 5), “Woe to Assyria, the rod of My anger.” And one should always pray that the Lord bring back all the transgressors of Israel in repentance, and that guilt not come about through him, and “when your enemy falls, do not rejoice,” for at a time when the wicked are in distress, the Divine Presence is distressed, as I have written above under the entry Love of Fellow Men.
Pele Yoetz 240:3: And every time his inclination entices him to transgress his Maker's commandment, let him strengthen himself like a lion with pure thoughts; let him persist in this and similar thoughts, press himself and push away his inclination. He should do this for all commandments that depend on the heart, such as “you shall not hate your brother in your heart,” “and you shall not stray after your heart,” etc., and the like — let a man be firm in strengthening himself against his inclination with thoughts of refraining from sinning against Him, and the Lord will not withhold good, and one who comes to purify himself is helped [from Heaven] (Shabbat 104a).
Pele Yoetz 241:1: Netilat Yadayim (Washing the Hands) — Washing the hands is a rabbinic commandment, and many unlearned people are lax about it — some do not wash at all and eat without washing hands, and some wash only their fingertips, or wash only one side of the hand, not being careful to turn the hands to every side, and there are several other laws that invalidate the washing, such as rings, water that has been used for work, human strength [applied vigorously], the touch of the washed hand by the unwashed hand requiring drying and rewashing, and dirt under the fingernails invalidating the washing, and the like. And the saying of our sages, of blessed memory, is known that one who treats hand-washing lightly deserves excommunication (Berachot 19a) and deserves death (Sotah 4b), and comes to poverty (Shabbat 62b), since the Hebrew word for hand-washing forms an acronym for “poor.” Therefore let one who is careful in his conduct be even more diligent, and be careful to know all the laws of hand-washing from books and from scholars, and be careful to wash his hands properly, and fill his hands with the Lord's blessing.
Pele Yoetz 241:2: And there is another washing that is more obligatory, namely, the washing of Mayim Acharonim [after the meal], which is a duty (Eruvin 17b; Chullin 105b), to the point that they exempted an army going out to war from washing the hands before the meal [due to lack of water], yet obligated them in Mayim Acharonim, because danger [from Sodomite salt] is more severe. And even nowadays, though Sodomite salt is not commonly found and there is no danger, nevertheless it is incumbent upon us to fulfill the words of the Sages, for if it does not blind the eyes of the flesh, it blinds the eyes of the intellect and the soul, for the beginning of all their words reaches to Heaven and their mystery is exalted and lofty. And people are also lax about this washing, and do not do Mayim Acharonim except when eating at the table in the company of the household, but if one eats his bread during the day in a shop, or while traveling, they are not careful, and thereby transgress. The God-fearing man should have in his shop, or when traveling, a vessel ready for washing and a vessel to catch the water, for Mayim Acharonim is only done with a vessel, and thereby he will be saved from all evil.
Pele Yoetz 241:3: There is also another washing that is likewise obligatory, namely, when eating something dipped in liquid, such as honey, water, wine, oil, or milk. And here too many unlearned people are lax and careful about it only on the night of Passover — “why is this night different?” Therefore the man who fears the word of the Lord should not be lax and should not transgress the words of the Sages at any time, and should not eat anything dipped in liquid without washing his hands. However, if he is cooking something like a preserve, yogurt, or a stewed dish and the like, and eats it with a spoon or fork, then washing is not required.
Pele Yoetz 241:4: Likewise for prayer, washing is required if one's attention was diverted, and they said (Pesachim 46a) that for prayer, one must walk up to four mil ahead if it is in front of him in order to wash his hands, and up to a mil behind he must return. And here too the masses are not careful. Likewise, if while studying he touched mucus from his nose or wax from his ear, or scratched his head, or touched covered parts of his body, he needs to wash for the honor of the Torah. Likewise, if this happens to him while eating bread, he needs to wash. And he should not approach to study, pray, bless, or eat with a body [that has become] impure [through such contact], for once his hands become impure, his whole body becomes impure. Let one who is careful in his conduct be even more diligent, for one who transgresses the Torah or the words of the Sages in light matters, requiring no great effort or expense, his punishment is heavier for not having taken to heart to fulfill the words of the Sages — this is a great principle. And the saying of our sages, of blessed memory, is known (Menachot 43b): greater is the punishment for [transgressing the law of] white [wool in tzitzit], etc., a parable of two men, etc. Therefore be careful with an easy commandment and flee from transgression, for God will bring everything into judgment, and one who keeps a commandment shall receive great reward.
Pele Yoetz 242:1: Nevelot HaPeh (Vulgar Speech) — The severity of vulgar speech is known, to the point that they said (Shabbat 33a) that whoever speaks vulgarly, even if a decree of seventy years for good has been sealed upon him, it is turned to evil for him, Heaven forbid. And it is written (Isaiah 9:16), “Therefore the Lord shall not rejoice in their young men, nor have mercy on their widows and orphans, for every mouth speaks vulgarity,” etc. And they said (Shabbat 33a) that Gehinnom is deepened for him. And even one who hears and remains silent bears sin and will surely be punished, as it is written (Proverbs 22:14), “He who is cursed by the Lord shall fall there.” Our sages, of blessed memory, elaborated at length on the punishment of one who speaks vulgar speech. And through our sins, this sin is found among the base, for base men are they and speak vulgarity, and the one who listens laughs along with them, when he should have protested against them — woe to them from the Day of Judgment.
Pele Yoetz 242:2: And I shall tell the generation what my own ears have heard: a story that happened in our days to a certain man who was a jester, always laughing and light-headed in the company of frivolous companions, speaking vulgar speech and the like, matters that caused laughter, levity and joy to empty and reckless men. And it happened one day, as his end drew near, that he lay dying and unconscious for several days, and in the middle of the night he opened his eyes like lightning and stood up and began to groan bitterly, “Woe, woe, what has befallen him?” and those standing over him were seized with trembling, and he began to say to them, “Do you not see the forms of black men, monstrous shapes, showing him inflated skins full of fire to pour into his mouth, and iron chains, and other harsh judgments prepared for him because he did much laughing and levity and vulgar speech?” And he cried out a great and bitter cry. And it happened that the matter became known throughout the city, and many people came, and to all of them he told these same things in a great cry of anguish. And when a man entered who had done as he had done, he would say to him, “You too did as I did; upon you too shall this cup pass.” And when someone entered who had heard him and remained silent and laughed, he would say to him, “Remember, on such-and-such a day you heard me speaking vulgarity and mockery, and where you should have struck me with a shoe across the face, you were silent and laughed — upon you too shall such a cup pass.” And he would cry out bitterly and describe the harsh judgments shown to him, and this continued for three days and three nights, until finally he put his hands into his mouth and opened his mouth wide beyond measure, crying, “Throw it, throw the fire!” and in the midst of this his soul departed, and all the people were aroused to repentance. Let every heart tremble at this.
Pele Yoetz 242:3: And included in vulgar speech are the remnants of gentile talk, for all their words are words of lewdness and vulgar speech, defiling the mouth and turning it into a piece of carrion — and how can such a mouth approach to serve the Lord, being a filthy vessel full of filth? Of this it is said (Psalms 50:16), “But to the wicked God says: What right have you to declare My statutes?”, Heaven forbid. Therefore let one who guards his soul distance himself from these and from hearing them, for their encounter is evil, and let him guard his mouth and his tongue, and not sit in the session of scoffers, guarding his soul from distress (Proverbs 21:23). In any case, he should not remain silent and withhold good — whoever heeds this, upon him shall come the blessing of good.
Pele Yoetz 243:1: Nekiyut (Cleanliness) — The essence of cleanliness is to be clean from sin, for sins are what defile and soil the soul, causing blemish and filth in the King's palace, the King of the world, and every transgression that a person commits leaves a mark on his soul and on the supernal worlds and on the Throne of Glory, and many such evils that our limited capacity to understand and grasp cannot fully comprehend. Therefore let a man tremble and take hold of himself, and be careful to be clean-handed of every hint of transgression; and if he sins, let him hasten to follow the paths of repentance and to atone for the sin against his soul, and let him do whatever is in his power to cleanse what he has blemished above, for if he does not hasten
Pele Yoetz 243:2: to cleanse and purify, the later punishment will be greater than the first, since he did not have regard for his Maker's honor in washing and cleaning that which soils His palace. More will be written on this below under the entry Teshuvah [Repentance], God willing.
Pele Yoetz 243:3: There is also a cleanliness that must be greatly heeded, namely, that one's body be clean within and without when standing to serve in the Name of the Lord, in prayers, blessings, and studies, for they said (Ta'anit 11a) that a person should always regard himself as though a holy one dwells within his intestines, meaning that he should keep his body clean. And they said (Berachot 23a) that one who needs to relieve himself should not pray, and if he prays, his prayer is an abomination. And one must also be careful externally that there be no filth at the anus, which invalidates prayer, and his garments too should be clean of all filth, and the place must also be clean of all filth and dirt and of any bad odor. And of one who is not careful about this it is written (Numbers 15:31), “That soul shall surely be cut off” for the word of the Lord which he has despised, Heaven have mercy. And this commandment is incumbent upon women wherever there are children, that she watch over the ways of her household (Proverbs 31:27), that it be always clean and that her children be clean — and if she is not careful, that woman shall bear her sin, and a woman who fears the Lord shall be praised (ibid., v. 30).
Pele Yoetz 243:4: Also included in the trait of cleanliness is that one be free of any stain and any dirt, and that his garments be clean and pressed, and that he not appear outside in dirty garments like one of the reckless, for this is not proper conduct. And the saying of our sages, of blessed memory, is known (Shabbat 114a) regarding the Torah scholar on whose garment a stain was found. And every person should make himself like a Torah scholar in this matter.
Pele Yoetz 244:1: Ne'emanut (Trustworthiness) — Trustworthiness is a faithful trait; it has become a cornerstone, and this is a great principle in the Torah: that a servant be trustworthy to his master, a hired worker to his employer, doing his work faithfully; that an agent be a faithful messenger to those who sent him, and especially agents of a commandment and all those hired for the work of Heaven, such as teachers of children, prayer leaders and the like, must be extra diligent to conduct themselves with complete trustworthiness and not to be unfaithful in their mission even the smallest amount, lest it be said of them, God forbid, “Cursed be he who does the Lord's work deceitfully” (Jeremiah 48:10). And employers too must be trustworthy toward their hired workers, keeping their eyes open regarding them and bringing them benefit, especially those engaged in the work of Heaven, who depend on the members of the community, and the members of the community depend on the One who spoke and the world came into being. In sum, this is a trait needed by every person: the worker shall perform his work completely, with all his heart and all his soul, and not turn aside after his own gain, but do what is incumbent upon him to do as is proper; and the employer shall open his hand generously. Likewise toward all who rely on him and wish to benefit from him, whether with his money, his body, his wisdom, or his counsel, he should not withhold any good that is in his power to do. And when he does it, let him do the favor completely, as a person does for himself, and not turn aside after his own gain, and the Lord will repay him.
Pele Yoetz 244:2: And now, through our sins, faithful men have vanished from among people, for every man turns to his own gain, and of this generation it is said (Micah 7:5), “Trust not in a friend, put no confidence in a companion,” and “even a brother will not truly redeem” (a common folk saying goes: “Everyone fends for himself”). And if in earlier times our sages, of blessed memory, already warned us and said (Derech Eretz Rabbah, ch. 5), “Judge every person as a potential robber, yet honor them like Rabban Gamliel,” how much more so now that men of trustworthiness have perished, and we have no one to rely and lean on except our Father in Heaven. However, if a trustworthy man, tried and tested, is found, let one hold fast to him and not let go, and even though he maintains a reputation for uprightness, let him make his righteousness and trustworthiness known, as we find with Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, who showed Israel the accounting of the Tabernacle's donations (Shemot Rabbah 51:2), for a man of trustworthiness abounds in blessings.
Pele Yoetz 245:1: Niddah — The severity involved is known. And in the holy Zohar (Shemot, p. 3) they treated it strictly and said: there is no impurity in the world like the impurity of a niddah, and as soon as a person draws near a niddah, impurity leaps upon him — this is what is written (Leviticus 15:24), “And her impurity shall be upon him.” And they forbade even excessive conversation with her (Avot DeRabbi Natan 2:1), and a mnemonic hint is fixed in “ne'elamti dumiyah hecheshaiti” [“I was silent, I held my peace”], whose initial letters form “niddah.” Likewise, one who gazes at her causes harm to himself, and likewise if she gazes upon a man, it is not good. And there are several laws and warnings that people are not careful about. And according to the care one takes in matters of holiness during the days of niddah, so he will merit a holy soul for the offspring, and the opposite, the opposite; and this is the cause of the many foolish children, corrupt children, unreliable children that are found.
Pele Yoetz 245:2: And a man who fears the Lord and fears for his own soul, lest he die and his best days be cut short, and who wishes to merit holy seed, should, as soon as he marries a wife or marries off his children, study thoroughly from books and from scholars to know what he should do, and be very careful to act according to the entire Torah, not deviating right or left, and thereby his offspring will be mighty in the land, a generation of the upright who shall be blessed. And they should not hand things from one hand to the other, even without touching, and should not toss things from one to the other. And she should not pour water on his hands, and they should not eat together from the same bowl, and there are several other matters that are utterly forbidden and criminal sins that people are not careful about — woe and alas, take this to heart.
Pele Yoetz 246:1: Nedarim (Vows) — The severity of vows is known, for through the sin of vows, a man's wife and children die (Shabbat 32b). And they said (Nedarim 22a) that one who makes a vow is as though he built a high place, and one who fulfills it is as though he offered a sacrifice upon it. They further said (Ta'anit 11a) that one who makes a vow is called a sinner. And now many women who make vows are common, and it is also found among men that one makes a vow before the ark. And the saying of our sages, of blessed memory, is known on the verse (Ecclesiastes 5:5), “Do not let your mouth bring your flesh into guilt, and do not say before the messenger that it was an error, lest God be angry at your voice and destroy the work of your hands” — which they explained regarding one who makes a vow before the ark and does not pay it, causing the death of his children and losing the few commandments in his possession. And this applies not only when one explicitly vows, but even if one says he will do some good deed, or observed some good custom without stipulating that it be without a vow, the obligation of a vow remains upon him.
Pele Yoetz 246:2: And the God-fearing and tenderhearted man should have it constantly on his lips to stipulate for everything that it be without a vow, and that even if he observes some good custom for extended periods, it not remain upon him as a binding vow, and that he be permitted to retract at any time he wishes. And if he vowed something for charity, he should not delay paying it, for he injures the soul of the angel created from that pledge, which hangs and stands waiting for his vow to be fulfilled. And since they said that one who makes a vow is as though he built a high place, and one who fulfills it is as though he offered a sacrifice upon it, thus if he has made a vow, let him hasten to find escape for himself and go to a sage to have it annulled, and afterward let what comes from his lips not change, and without a vow let him do whatever comes from his mouth if he can — this is the straight path.
Pele Yoetz 247:1: Nes (Miracle) — Our sages, of blessed memory, warned us (Shabbat 32a) that a person should not rely on a miracle, lest no miracle be done for him, and if a miracle is done for him, it is deducted from his merits. And truly, the miracles that the Holy One, blessed be He, performs for us in His mercy and kindness at every moment, since we are like a single lamb among many wolves, and were it not for the Lord who was with us, we would have been swallowed alive. And our sages, of blessed memory, said (Niddah 31a) on the verse (Psalms 136:4), “To Him who alone does great wonders,” that the one for whom the miracle is done does not recognize his own miracle, for many people suffer harsh afflictions, great blows, and serious, chronic illnesses, and if miracles are done for them and they are saved, their mouths are filled with praise — they thank the Lord for His kindness and His wonders to the children of man. How much more so is it a doubled and redoubled good that the Omnipresent does for us when He grants us health, quiet and tranquility with no evil affliction at all. Of this they said (Yalkut Shimoni, Psalms 150:6), “Let every soul praise the Lord” — a person is obligated to praise for every single breath that saved him from serious illnesses and from all the evils stirring to come upon the world; and even if our mouths were full of song, etc., we could not sufficiently praise Him. And if our father Jacob, peace be upon him, said (Genesis 32:11), “I am unworthy of all the kindnesses and all the truth,” what shall we answer and what shall we say? At least let us flee from relying on a miracle as much as we can, for we have few commandments and merits in our possession, and if they are deducted from us for miracles, we are utterly naked, and our departure will be like our entrance, without merits, God forbid. And if a person relies on a miracle for the sake of monetary gain, this is foolish and senseless, an exchange for the worse, like one who trades a pearl and a precious stone for a lump of dirt. And if no miracle is done for him, he has endangered his own life, and he is destined to give account, close to one who destroys himself knowingly; and if he brings himself into a place of danger, he transgresses what the Torah said (Deuteronomy 4:15), “And you shall greatly guard your souls” — the Merciful One was precise and said “greatly,” to teach that one must be careful and take heed even of a remote doubt and concern where there is reason to fear danger. And whoever transgresses the word of the Merciful One will surely be punished, either in this world or in the World to Come. And they said in the holy Zohar (part 1, p. 199 approx.) on the verse (Proverbs 22:3), “A prudent man sees evil and hides himself, but the simple pass on and are punished” — that even if he has no other transgression, but only that he transgressed by not hiding himself, for this alone he is punished. And guarding one's soul is a fitting commandment to protect and save one from every trouble.
Pele Yoetz 248:1: Nisayon (Trial) — Behold, we pray before the Lord every day, “Do not bring us into trial,” and the intent is that He not incite against us the bear — that is, the evil inclination — with a double enticement to make us transgress our own understanding and our Maker's will, as He tried King David, peace be upon him, or that He not try us with harsh afflictions and the pinches of poverty and the like, as He tried Job. But in any case, there is no person whom the Holy One, blessed be He, does not try — the rich man through his wealth, the poor man through his poverty, the wise man through his wisdom, the sufferer through his suffering, the merchant through his business, and the craftsman through his craft. And every day, every hour, every moment, he stands in trial, as his inclination grows and renews itself against him to make him commit a transgression, or to neglect a commandment in thought, speech, or deed, and he must be mighty in subduing his inclination (Avot 4:1), to withstand the trial and withdraw his hand from every hint of transgression, to fulfill every good thing properly, and this requires great strength, with great vigor.
Pele Yoetz 248:2: Thus, since trial is unavoidable, how good it is to pour out speech before our merciful God that if He brings us into trial, He help us for the sake of the honor of His Name to withstand the trial. And let the Israelite servant say, “I love my Master, and I wish with a whole heart to be afflicted with the afflictions of Job, and more than these, for the sake of the honor of His Name, only that nothing distract me from His service, from engaging in His Torah, and from clinging to Him,” as Rabbi Akiva said, “All my days I have been troubled, wondering when it would come to my hand and I could fulfill it” (Yerushalmi Berachot 9:5), precisely so. Therefore, how good it is to ask, after every prayer and every supplication, that He do with us what is good in His eyes for His service and for delight before His Throne of Glory and for the repair of the sparks of holiness.
Pele Yoetz 249:1: Nesech (Libation Wine) — The severity of the prohibition against wine used for idolatrous libation is explained by the halachic authorities, and especially in the book “Yayin HaMeshamer,” which brings several bans, excommunications, and curses from several great rabbinical authorities of the world on this matter — it makes a person's hair stand on end. And through our sins, great potential for error exists in the lands of Edom, because they have servants in gentile households, and it is impossible to escape the touch of their hand and the wine being out of sight; and there are also those who make wine in distant villages and produce it in abundance, and those who go to produce it are ignorant and lacking fear of Heaven, and are not careful about the involvement of gentile hands or about keeping the wine out of sight, or about letting the many stay overnight [unsupervised with the wine]. For all this, the God-fearing man should guard his soul, for it is a grave transgression, having a trace of idolatry, and one transgression drags another, for they have written that we have a tradition that whoever stumbles into the prohibition of wine removes the image of God from his face, and has no share in the World to Come, and eventually stumbles into [the sins abbreviated as] NaShGaZ [niddah, a gentile maidservant, a gentile woman, a harlot], Heaven have mercy. And one of true feeling should be wary even of a remote concern and fulfill the verse (Proverbs 23:2), “And put a knife to your throat if you are a man of appetite.”
Pele Yoetz 250:1: Nefesh (Soul) — Let every person of true feeling hold his soul precious in his own eyes and not worry about his money, so as not to sin against his soul and in order to merit his soul, for all that a man has he will give for his life. And let him make himself cruel like a raven toward his own body and toward his children and household members in order to merit his soul, for the body perishes and is lost like a passing shadow, and all bodily pleasures are only for the moment, mere vanity, an illusion, while the soul shall return to God, and the fruit of one's deeds shall be eaten according to his actions, whether good or evil, and there is the true delight, the true honor, and the true punishment, hundreds of years [long], according to the scale and balance of justice in the hand of the God of knowledge, the Lord. And we are strangers in this world, like a traveler who turns aside to lodge for the night at an inn, who does not worry about anything until he comes to his own house — so must a person conduct himself all the days he is in this world, and should worry only about meriting his soul for the World to Come, for that is his true home.
Pele Yoetz 250:2: And one who merits to love the Lord with a true love as is fitting will not worry even about his own soul within him, but only about his true soul, which is the Holy One, blessed be He, who is the soul of souls, in the manner explained in the holy Zohar (part 3, p. 67) on the verse that is written (Isaiah 26:9), “My soul longs for You in the night.” And let his heart burn with fire to give delight to his Creator specifically, to the point that if he were to enter the hypothetical scenario where, by transgressing every transgression, he would merit life in the World to Come, and by performing commandments and good deeds he would inherit Gehinnom, God forbid, he would choose death over life in order to give delight to his Creator, for better is one hour of Torah and good deeds, and that the exalted, uplifted, awesome and terrible King, the King of Glory, whose greatness is beyond measure, be pleased to receive delight from us who are nothing — is this not far better than all the life of the World to Come? And when we ask to merit and live and inherit good and blessing for life in the World to Come, this too, as the verse says (Psalms 30:13), “That glory [i.e., the Divine Presence] may sing praise to You,” meaning the Shechinah, in such a way that everything leads to one place: to give delight to our Creator. This should be the aim of our entire lives, and this is the whole of man.
Pele Yoetz 251:1: Nitzu'ach (Winning/Being Victorious) — The love of winning — this trait belongs to the enemies of Israel [a euphemism]; let their hand wither, for it delays the coming of the Messiah. It is what causes suspicion among Torah scholars and all the strife, hatred, rivalry, quarrel and dispute in the world — all comes from the love of winning. Do you not see that if a man goes to a sage to seek God's guidance on matters of prohibition and permission, he accepts the ruling upon himself at once with love, even if it costs him a thousand thousand gold coins, and does not open his mouth to chirp, but rather says, “Let Israel say, blessed is He who gave us a Torah of truth” — happy is Israel! But if there is a dispute between men, even over the value of a mere perutah, and they approach for judgment and are judged, the one who loses the case increases the strife, and enmity is set with the judge and with his litigant opponent, and how much money and how many lives are sunk into matters of slander, and they become factions upon factions, groups upon groups, until the flame of the fire of strife rises and cannot be extinguished, since each faction raises itself up saying, “Ours is victorious,” and “why should I lower myself and remain beneath my fellow?” Would that they gain wisdom to understand what winning or being the victor gives or adds — truth shows its own way, and “the acknowledgment of the Rabbis is itself their praise.” And our holy sages, of blessed memory, used to say before the assembled congregation of Israel, “The words I said before you were an error on my part” (Shabbat 63b).
Pele Yoetz 251:2: And even if it seems to him in his innocence that the truth is with him and his colleagues have strayed from the path of reason, he should not thrust himself with great vigor to establish his own view; rather, it is better that he humble himself and be the victor by seeking peace and increasing peace, for by this he is called a true victor — one who conquers his own inclination and subdues his own spirit. And what does it matter to him to prevail over a man like himself, who is like a mere breath? It is better, and he shall be called a hero, that he prevail over a great, terrible and mighty king — that is, Satan, that is, the evil inclination — who, through such strategies and vanities, wages war with him to cast him into the pit of destruction. And if he prevails over his inclination in this matter, this is his honor, and he will merit great honor, for the reward is according to the pain — he shall rise higher and higher.
